coursesExamined.name: Personal & Professional Development
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
coursesExamined.contribution: Year 1 academic writing, research literacy, civic engagement and personal development.

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Economics
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
coursesExamined.contribution: establishes economic reasoning about markets, incentives and aggregate outcomes within the cross-disciplinary core

coursesExamined.name: Research Methods & Statistics
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
coursesExamined.contribution: provides research design, quantitative analysis and statistics for interdisciplinary inquiry

coursesExamined.name: Governance of Sustainability
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines how institutions, participation and policy shape collective sustainability decisions

coursesExamined.name: Conservation Biology
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces conservation biology through biodiversity loss, its human causes and possible responses. Students examine habitat destruction and fragmentation, overharvesting, invasive species, climate change, disasters and extinction, followed by conservation planning, species management and conservation in altered landscapes. A local threatened-species project investigates conservation status and protection measures and develops a public-awareness flyer.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines biodiversity loss, conservation strategies and the interaction between ecological evidence and human choices

coursesExamined.name: The Science of Evolution
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines evolutionary theory from genetic mechanisms to the diversification and history of life. Students study natural selection, variation and drift, population and quantitative genetics, adaptation and sexual reproduction, then species concepts, speciation, phylogeny and macroevolution. Genomics, development, biogeography and coevolution extend the account across scales. A project reconstructs a chosen species' evolutionary history using Tinbergen's four questions.
coursesExamined.contribution: Explains evolutionary mechanisms, variation, adaptation, phylogeny and diversification through an independently researched species history. It complements the biological strand without claiming a dedicated human-health focus.

coursesExamined.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Develops ecological principles from organisms and populations to communities and ecosystems. Environmental conditions, resources and life cycles frame competition, feeding relationships, selection, population dynamics and biodiversity. Energy and matter cycles connect ecological processes to conservation and human impacts. Dedicated practical sessions teach simple ecological modelling in R, and a small research project communicates findings through a poster.
coursesExamined.contribution: develops ecological understanding of organisms, populations, communities and ecosystems

coursesExamined.name: Sustainable Farming & Innovation
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines how food production can balance human needs with environmental impacts. Students assess current agriculture, horticulture and animal husbandry, their effects on biodiversity and ecosystems, and alternative practices and innovations. Aquaculture, alternative animal-protein sources and farming for other industries extend the comparison. A literature-based project critically investigates a chosen sustainable-farming question and reports the evidence without prescribing a single preferred approach.
coursesExamined.contribution: Critically compares food-production systems, ecological impacts and agricultural innovations through literature-based inquiry.

coursesExamined.name: Law, Society & Justice
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.
coursesExamined.contribution: introduces legal institutions, justice and the relationship between law and society

coursesExamined.name: Modern History
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines political, social and cultural transformations in modern history

coursesExamined.name: Histories of Gender
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies gendered histories and lives in North America from the nineteenth century to the present, centering storytelling and intersectionality. Queer and heteronormative narratives connect slavery, family, sexuality, health, incarceration and contemporary backlash to resistance and activism. Students interpret primary sources and scholarship, interview older queer people, contribute to the Walking with Pride activist artwork, and conduct an original research project in a chosen format.
coursesExamined.contribution: uses gender as a historical category to analyse institutions, inequality and social change

coursesExamined.name: Researching the “American Century”
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.
coursesExamined.contribution: Develops historical questions, critical engagement with sources, methodological rigour and a substantial research paper through the current American Century course. The archived Walcheren outline is not evidence for this course.

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Public International Law
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces public international law through its sources, theories, institutions and relationship to domestic legal systems. Legal principles are applied to responsibility, force, armed conflict, international crime, human rights, economic relations and environmental protection. The later course examines self-determination, Third World approaches, soft law, compliance and treaty politics. Case exercises develop legal reasoning, while a research podcast critically investigates a political dimension of international law.
coursesExamined.contribution: develops public-international-law analysis of states, institutions, rights and cross-border obligations

coursesExamined.name: Principles of Private Law
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines property, tort and contract law through comparison of legal systems, primarily Germany, France, England, China and the United States. Students analyze rights and obligations, ownership, nuisance, negligence, contract formation and fairness, remedies and related policy pressures. Legal issue briefs apply the IRAC method. An issue-based comparative contract-law paper and simulated mediation develop comparative analysis, legal argument and negotiation.
coursesExamined.contribution: Develops comparative property, tort and contract law, legal issue analysis, mediation and research into a contract-law question.

coursesExamined.name: Foundations of European Union Law
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces the EU legal order through its institutions, sources, competences and relationship to member-state law. Students study supremacy, legal effect, liability and judicial remedies before applying citizenship and free-movement law to concrete problems. Structured legal cases and research into current judgments develop interpretation and comparison across EU and domestic settings. Digital regulation and the green transition provide a contemporary application.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines EU institutions, legal authority and the relationship between European and national law

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces major philosophical questions through close study of arguments from ancient Greek thought to contemporary philosophy, with a related Buddhist perspective on the self. Students examine knowledge, ethics, God, mind and consciousness, freedom, identity, time and meaning. Historical texts and contemporary debates, including AI consciousness and concepts of race and gender, develop the ability to reconstruct, evaluate and formulate philosophical arguments in focused essays.
coursesExamined.contribution: provides philosophical foundations for analysing knowledge, reality, ethics and human life

coursesExamined.name: Ethics
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
coursesExamined.contribution: develops normative reasoning about moral problems, responsibility and competing principles

coursesExamined.name: Philosophy of Emotion
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines what emotions are and how they shape knowledge, decision-making, ethics, social life and politics. Feeling, cognitive and perceptual theories are compared with historical, phenomenological and contemporary accounts. Love, fear, grief, moods and political anger provide focused cases, alongside emotions in art and their changing relation to time. Students analyze texts and emotional vignettes and develop an independent philosophical paper or a project combining argument with creative work.
coursesExamined.contribution: connects philosophical analysis of emotion with questions about mind, agency and human experience

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.
coursesExamined.contribution: introduces political concepts and normative arguments about authority, freedom, equality and justice

coursesExamined.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces empirical comparison of political systems, with democracy, democratization and autocratization as central concerns. Students study political institutions, rules, actors and behaviour, including parties, elections, participation, polarization, interest groups and policy. Research exercises operationalize and measure democracy using V-Dem data and compare academic literature-search tools. A qualitative or quantitative research memo answers a theoretically grounded comparative-politics question through empirical analysis.
coursesExamined.contribution: compares political institutions and systems using concepts and empirical evidence

coursesExamined.name: Theory of International Relations
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces international relations and geopolitics through competing theoretical approaches and historical and contemporary cases. Students study realism, liberalism, Marxism, constructivism, critical theory and foreign-policy analysis. Case research connects theories to conflicts, colonial relationships, economic competition and climate politics. A UN Security Council simulation requires country-position research, strategy and position papers, negotiation and collaborative resolution drafting.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines major theories of international relations and their explanations of global order and conflict

coursesExamined.name: European Union Politics
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.
coursesExamined.contribution: analyses European Union institutions, integration and political decision-making

coursesExamined.name: Peace & Conflict
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines causes and dynamics of conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies are connected to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. Students compare travelling concepts across disciplines, produce an interdisciplinary podcast, and develop an evidence-based policy brief with a research dossier. Positionality reflection addresses how assumptions shape inquiry.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines causes of armed conflict and approaches to peace, security and conflict resolution

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Sociology
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
coursesExamined.contribution: introduces sociological analysis of institutions, identities, inequality and social interaction

coursesExamined.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
coursesExamined.contribution: develops qualitative research design, data collection, interpretation and reflexive analysis

coursesExamined.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.
coursesExamined.contribution: Studies civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial theory, with research on civic organisations, movements or initiatives.

coursesExamined.name: Epidemiology & Public Health
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces epidemiological reasoning and its application to public health. Students measure and interpret disease patterns, study research designs, association, bias, confounding and causality, then examine health determinants, promotion, needs assessment and screening. A local project analyzes a Zeeland health challenge, compares population data, considers affected groups and interventions, and incorporates stakeholder perspectives into feasible recommendations.
coursesExamined.contribution: introduces epidemiology, population health and the social distribution and prevention of disease

coursesExamined.name: Pharmacology
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies how drugs act at molecular, cellular and whole-body levels and how the body handles them. Pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, metabolism, toxicity and pharmacogenomics provide foundations for rational therapies and drug-target identification. Applications emphasize nervous-system drugs, antimicrobial treatment and inflammatory, immune and airway conditions. Quantitative exercises and virtual experiments model drug responses, while a psychoactive-drug project proposes a testable follow-up experiment.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines how medicines act on biological systems and how therapeutic effects and risks are evaluated

coursesExamined.name: Infection & Immunity
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines host-microbe interactions and the immune mechanisms that protect against infection or cause disease. Microbiology and innate defence lead into antibodies, antigen recognition, lymphocyte development and memory, effector responses and mucosal immunity. Vaccination, allergy, immunodeficiency and autoimmunity connect mechanisms to clinical problems. Students analyze lymphocyte phenotypes using original flow-cytometry data and synthesize recent research in an extended and graphical abstract.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines pathogens, immune responses and the biological mechanisms of infection

coursesExamined.name: Mechanisms of Disease
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Connects normal organ function to pathophysiology across digestive, cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine and nervous systems. Students integrate anatomy and physiology to explain symptoms, disease mechanisms, diagnostic findings, treatment and prognosis. Published clinical cases develop differential reasoning and appraisal of diagnostic procedures. A creative assignment constructs an imaginary disease whose symptoms, mechanism and proposed treatment must form a coherent pathophysiological account.
coursesExamined.contribution: connects cellular and physiological dysfunction to the mechanisms and clinical expression of disease

coursesExamined.name: Neurobiology
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies nervous systems and behaviour from comparative, evolutionary and physiological perspectives. Brain anatomy and laboratory introductions support analysis of animal behaviour, research models and welfare. The second part connects regulatory behaviour and biological rhythms to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based disorder report apply neurobiological concepts while animal-research assignments examine reduction, refinement and replacement.
coursesExamined.contribution: provides neurobiological foundations for understanding brain organisation and behaviour

coursesExamined.name: Perception & Action
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines neural and psychological processes underlying perception and action

coursesExamined.name: Higher Order Functions
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Deepens understanding of neuroanatomy, neurophysiology and the experimental study of higher cognitive functions. Students examine attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness, connecting brain function and dysfunction to behaviour. An attentional-blink experiment provides direct engagement with empirical work. A team research proposal requires literature analysis, a feasible experimental design and ethical reflection, supported by peer review.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines higher cognitive functions and their neural bases

coursesExamined.name: Psycholinguistics
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
coursesExamined.contribution: connects language processing with cognition, psychology and neuroscience

coursesExamined.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Students study biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, enzymes and energy metabolism, cell division, DNA and heredity, gene expression, genomes and biotechnology. Scientific experiments and papers are analyzed through short teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium. A responsive final component selects additional life- and biomedical-science topics with the class.
coursesExamined.contribution: Introduces molecular and cellular foundations, heredity, gene expression, biotechnology and scientific-paper analysis. Integrated human physiology is supplied by the separate Human Physiology course, rather than assumed here.

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
coursesExamined.contribution: introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of brain and behaviour

coursesExamined.name: Molecular Cell Biology
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies the molecular mechanisms underlying cellular structure, physiology and regulation, primarily in eukaryotes. Bioenergetics, proteins and membranes connect to genome replication, repair and gene expression, followed by trafficking, signalling, division, tissues, stem cells and cancer. Students evaluate research methods and reproducibility and investigate a drug's molecular target, therapeutic action, metabolism and adverse effects through primary literature, a paper and a research poster.
coursesExamined.contribution: develops molecular and cellular explanations of life processes

coursesExamined.name: Human Physiology
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies normal function and regulation in the adult human body, linking molecular and cellular processes to integrated organ systems. Homeostasis, signalling and energy handling frame nervous, endocrine, muscular, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, digestive and reproductive functions. Medical examples illustrate physiological principles. An individual literature-based paper examines a selected physiological or pathophysiological process and is developed through structured peer review and revision.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines integrated human physiological systems and their regulation

coursesExamined.name: Biochemistry
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines the chemistry of life, emphasizing biomolecular structure and function, enzymes and metabolic pathways. Students study proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, enzyme kinetics and regulation, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, the citric-acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation and further carbohydrate, lipid and nitrogen metabolism. Protein-biochemistry techniques are discussed. A literature-based disease project links a biochemical defect to symptoms, diagnostics and treatment, keeping the molecular mechanism central.
coursesExamined.contribution: explains the molecular chemistry and metabolic processes that sustain living systems

coursesExamined.name: Life Science Laboratory
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Provides hands-on training in biochemical, microbiological and molecular laboratory methods. Blood analysis, microbial culture and hygiene lead into bacterial transformation, green fluorescent protein production and purification, DNA isolation and analysis, and introductory bioinformatics. Students follow and sometimes adapt protocols, interpret experimental results, maintain reproducible laboratory records and communicate findings in scientific reports and figures.
coursesExamined.contribution: develops experimental laboratory practice for investigating biological questions

coursesExamined.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Connects cellular pathology with the genetic mechanisms of human disease. Students examine injury and death, inflammation and repair, neoplasia and lymphoid malignancies, then inheritance, genetic variation, epigenetics, molecular diagnosis and genetic treatment. Ethical, legal and safety questions accompany genetic technologies. A two-year research-grant proposal integrates literature, hypotheses, method selection, controls, feasibility and budgeting; an ethics debate examines stakeholder positions.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying human disease

coursesExamined.name: Social Psychology
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.
coursesExamined.contribution: uses psychological evidence to analyse social influence, groups and interpersonal behaviour

coursesExamined.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
coursesExamined.contribution: develops experimental design, statistical inference and interpretation for behavioural research

coursesExamined.name: Psychopathology
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines mental health and psychopathology across the lifespan using a biopsychosocial perspective. Historical views, classification and assessment frame biological, psychological, cultural and social explanations of disorders and treatment. Case-based work applies diagnostic concepts to varied presentations. A structured literature-based essay investigates a focused mental-health question through explicit searching, source selection, evidence appraisal and synthesis, with optional use of PRISMA reporting tools.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines psychological disorders, explanatory models and evidence-based approaches to mental health

coursesExamined.name: Medical & Health Psychology
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines health and illness through interactions among biological, psychological and sociocultural factors. Health inequalities, behaviour and prevention lead into stress, symptoms, pain, medical consultation and treatment decisions. Chronic illness is considered from patients', families' and healthcare professionals' perspectives. Students analyze research, interventions and clinical cases, practice interviewing with attention to culture, and apply clinical-health formulation to understand support and quality of life in medical settings.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines psychological processes in health, illness, prevention and behaviour change

coursesExamined.name: Psychodiagnostics & Psychotherapies
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces clinical psychological assessment and major psychotherapeutic approaches across the lifespan. Students study ethics, diagnostic systems, test reliability and validity, interviews, personality and cognitive assessment, then psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic, systemic and integrative treatments. Training sessions develop introductory administration, scoring and interpretation skills. A psychodiagnostic case report integrates findings and treatment recommendations, while self-monitoring examines developing clinical skills.
coursesExamined.contribution: develops evidence-based understanding of psychological assessment and therapeutic interventions

coursesExamined.name: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Teaches systematic review and meta-analysis for synthesizing evidence in medical, behavioural and related research. Students define review questions, search and select studies, extract and code findings, assess bias and compute effect sizes. Hands-on R work fits fixed- and random-effects models, examines heterogeneity and moderators, conducts meta-regression and investigates publication bias. A group project completes a small meta-analysis and presents its methods and results in a research poster.
coursesExamined.contribution: synthesises psychological, medical and social research through systematic reviews, meta-analysis and hands-on R analysis; this is evidence synthesis rather than a new primary-data study

coursesExamined.name: Lifespan Developmental Psychology
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines physical, cognitive, emotional, social and personality development from prenatal life through old age and death. Biological and environmental influences are considered alongside attachment, education, relationships, cultural differences and developmental psychopathology. Students connect theoretical perspectives to case studies, assessment and interventions at different life stages. A life-story interview with an adult over fifty applies developmental concepts through interviewing, analysis and a written report.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines psychological development across the lifespan and its biological and social influences

coursesExamined.name: Communicating the Climate Crisis
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines how climate knowledge, uncertainty and responsibility are communicated in public culture

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Western Art History
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice. Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change, with sustained attention to the close examination of paintings. Practical assignments develop analysis of composition, space, form, tone and colour. A term paper studies a painting on location, combining visual interpretation with art-historical evidence and terminology.
coursesExamined.contribution: introduces methods for interpreting art and visual culture in historical context

coursesExamined.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines modern and contemporary art from the late nineteenth century to the present together with the institutions that shape its display and reception. Students study avant-gardes, abstraction, modernist design, figuration, postmodern and conceptual practices, and global contemporary art. Museums, exhibitions, curatorial choices and Eurocentric narratives are treated critically. An independently researched paper develops a focused art-historical question, methods and evidence-based argument.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines modern art, museums and the institutions that shape cultural meaning

coursesExamined.name: Writing Art's Histories
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines art-historical theory, historiography and methods of interpretation; this supports critical cultural inquiry rather than certifying an independent research project

coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation through fiction, poetry, drama and contemporary nonfiction, with an introductory component on film adaptation. Students investigate literary value and the constructed character of texts, using concepts of plot, character, setting, point of view, symbolism, style and form. Close reading and engagement with critical sources support analytical presentations and an essay or extended book review.
coursesExamined.contribution: introduces close reading, literary interpretation and critical analysis of cultural texts

coursesExamined.name: Great Literary Works
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Surveys major literary works from ancient epic to modern and later fiction, connecting literary form to questions of humanity, mortality, gender, freedom, community and civilization. Students compare genres and recurring motifs through works including Gilgamesh, Greek tragedy, confessional writing, framed tales, philosophical satire, colonial narratives and modernist fiction. Text-focused analysis and engagement with criticism develop interpretation of theme, technique and cultural context.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines major literary works across periods and cultures through close reading and comparative interpretation

coursesExamined.name: Life & Travel Writing
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies life narrative in literature and popular culture, including memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel writing and digital self-presentation. Memory, experience, identity, embodiment and agency frame debates about autobiographical truth, fiction, ethics, trauma and cultural positioning. Close readings connect popular, intellectual and migrant memoirs to theory. Students apply analytical concepts in a personal writing portfolio and an independent comparative or focused life-narrative project.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines how travel and life writing construct identities, places and cross-cultural encounters

coursesExamined.name: Media & Race
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.
coursesExamined.contribution: analyses how media represent and construct race, power and identity

coursesExamined.name: The Documentary
coursesExamined.evidenceRead: Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production. Students analyze nonfiction representation in historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts, from early and Soviet filmmaking through direct cinema and contemporary forms. Topics include propaganda, advocacy, ethnography, history, nature, audio and interactive documentary. Production workshops guide a short film through preproduction, filming and postproduction, with reflection on interviewing and representational choices.
coursesExamined.contribution: examines documentary form, evidence and representation through critical and creative analysis

finding: All 57 current course contributions are reconsidered from actual profiles or descriptions. Three internally coherent LAS concepts remain provisional: broad interdisciplinary society/culture/science, society/power/culture, and life/mind/health. Their programme priorities and 16/17/23-course pairwise differences are substantive. Final comparability and candidate stopping decisions remain dependent on a valid external cohort pathway.

descriptionOnly: The current American Century description supports source criticism, research design and a substantial paper; it does not establish the archived Walcheren project.
